top.why: The reference standard. Largest body of controlled evidence of any tinnitus treatment (Cochrane 2020: 28 studies, 2,733 participants), guideline-recommended, safe, and confirmed by the 2025 UNITI trial as among the most effective single treatments.

detail.strongest: Cochrane 2020 meta-analysis (28 RCTs, N=2,733): consistent quality-of-life benefit vs every comparator; UNITI 2025 head-to-head confirmation.
detail.weakest: No effect on loudness; most underlying trials are low-certainty with little long-term follow-up.
detail.studies: 28 randomized trials in the Cochrane review plus UNITI (N=461) and multiple iCBT RCTs.
detail.replication: Extensive — replicated across countries, formats and independent groups for two decades.
detail.loudness: None shown — Cochrane found only 'generally weak (if any)' loudness effects.
detail.distress: Strong — SMD −0.56 vs no treatment (≈11 THI points lower), the field's most reliable effect.
detail.availability: Available now through psychologists and digital programs; access limited mainly by therapist supply.
detail.uncertainty: Whether benefits persist long-term after therapy ends (few 6–12-month follow-ups).

top.couldChange: Would drop only if a treatment shows durable loudness reduction in large independent RCTs; could rise in absolute impact as digital delivery widens access.

top.why: Authorized, available, and consistent across three large trials and two real-world cohorts — which outweighs any single unreplicated trial, even though no Lenire study has ever had a sham arm and all of them are manufacturer-funded.

detail.strongest: Three large trials (N=326/191/112) plus two US real-world cohorts showing consistent within-arm THI improvement; FDA De Novo authorization DEN210033 (the only device in the bimodal tinnitus-treatment class).
detail.weakest: No trial has ever included a sham or no-treatment arm, and the pivotal trial's full-cohort primary endpoint was NOT achieved — the authorization rests on the moderate-or-worse subgroup.
detail.studies: TENT-A1, TENT-A2, TENT-A3 and two US chart reviews — every one manufacturer-funded or manufacturer-linked.
detail.replication: Replicated across its own cohorts, but nothing independent — an academic bimodal trial (Trinity College Dublin, NCT07393880) is recruiting.
detail.loudness: None shown — all endpoints are THI, a distress/handicap instrument.
detail.distress: Moderate — consistent within-arm improvements; sham-free designs mean placebo/natural course can't be excluded.
detail.availability: Available by prescription in the US (≈$4,000 self-pay, rarely insured) and Europe.
detail.uncertainty: How much of the effect is placebo/natural course — unanswerable without a sham-controlled trial.

top.couldChange: An independent sham-controlled RCT confirming benefit would cement it; failure to separate from sound therapy in independent hands would drop it.

top.why: The only tinnitus treatment with rigorous randomized evidence of reducing the tinnitus percept itself — loudness matching was a CO-PRIMARY endpoint, double-blinded and NIH-funded. Held below Lenire because it is one single-center trial, in one subtype, with no replication, no registered pivotal trial, and no visible path to market.

detail.strongest: Double-blind randomized crossover (JAMA Network Open 2023, N=99): co-primary loudness matching improved up to −14.1 dB (per-protocol, cumulative) alongside clinically meaningful TFI reduction, vs an active auditory-only control.
detail.weakest: Single-center, somatic-tinnitus subtype only, per-protocol n=56, and zero regulatory or commercial progress since 2023.
detail.studies: One pilot (N=20, 2018) and one main crossover RCT (N=99, 2023), both from the same lab.
detail.loudness: The strongest percept-level result in any tinnitus RCT (dB-matched loudness, co-primary endpoint).
detail.distress: TFI −13.2 per-protocol; 65% PP / 53% ITT responders vs 25%/20% control.
detail.availability: Not available anywhere; no trial sponsored by Auricle Inc is registered.
detail.uncertainty: Whether it ever reaches a pivotal trial, and whether results generalize beyond somatic tinnitus.

top.couldChange: A registered pivotal trial or FDA submission would push it up; continued company silence or a failed replication would drop it further.

top.why: CBT's evidence, delivered at scale. Kalmeda RCT (N=187, d=1.1 vs delayed treatment), the first double-blind sham-app-controlled trial (Japan 2026: THI −20.4 between groups), Oto RCTs, and Germany's DiGA listing make this the fastest-maturing category.

detail.strongest: Multiple positive RCTs across independent products, including the first double-blind sham-app-controlled trial (JAMA Otolaryngology 2026, per its authors).
detail.weakest: Category is heterogeneous — most apps on the market have no evidence; key trials are small, waitlist-controlled, or manufacturer-sponsored.
detail.studies: Kalmeda (N=187), Kyorin sham-controlled (N=60), Oto (N=96), Beukes iCBT (N=158), plus others.
detail.replication: Good at category level (several independent products/groups); limited per-product.
detail.loudness: None shown — all primary outcomes are distress instruments.
detail.distress: Strong — but note control types differ: d=1.1 was against delayed treatment, not sham.
detail.availability: Available now via app stores; Kalmeda prescribable in Germany; SilentCloud 510(k)-cleared (as a masker).
detail.uncertainty: The unpublished DEFINE trial (app vs human therapist) will show whether apps can substitute for clinicians.

top.couldChange: Peer-reviewed publication of the DEFINE non-inferiority trial could push it up; failed replications would trim it.

top.why: For people with severe hearing loss who qualify, CI is one of the few interventions with percept-level effects: tinnitus decreases in 25–72% of implanted patients and is completely suppressed in 8–45% (Ramakers 2015); pooled THI −14.0 across 28 studies.

detail.strongest: 2024 meta-analysis of 28 studies (N=853) plus consistent replication across many independent implant centers, covering both distress and percept-level ratings.
detail.weakest: All observational — nobody is randomized to implantation for tinnitus; benefit is entangled with hearing restoration; 0–25% worsen and ~9% develop new-onset tinnitus.
detail.studies: 28 cohort studies pooled; prospective series (e.g., UMC Utrecht) ongoing.
detail.loudness: Moderate — complete suppression in 8–45% of patients across studies (percept-level).
detail.availability: Available and usually insurance-covered — but only for qualifying severe hearing loss.
detail.uncertainty: Who improves vs who worsens, and durability over years.

top.couldChange: Applies only to implant candidates; better prediction of who improves (and who worsens) would strengthen its position.

top.why: Guideline-recommended ('Recommendation' strength) when hearing loss accompanies tinnitus; in the 2025 UNITI trial hearing aids were among the largest single-treatment effects. Honest basis: guideline consensus plus UNITI — Cochrane found the placebo-controlled evidence insufficient.

detail.strongest: UNITI 2025 (N=461): among the largest single-treatment effects; AAO-HNSF 'Recommendation' (middle strength tier — sound therapy gets only 'Option').
detail.weakest: Cochrane 2018: insufficient controlled evidence; tinnitus benefit hard to separate from hearing benefit.
detail.studies: UNITI head-to-head plus a large observational literature; thin on placebo-controlled designs.
detail.loudness: Limited — reduced audibility/awareness reported; controlled percept evidence weak.
detail.distress: Moderate — consistent severity reductions when hearing loss coexists (consensus + UNITI, low-certainty trial base).
detail.availability: Widely available; OTC from ~$200 (incl. FDA-authorized AirPods hearing-aid software since 2024).
detail.uncertainty: How much is tinnitus-specific vs simply hearing better.

top.couldChange: A well-controlled trial isolating the tinnitus effect from the hearing benefit would settle the score either way.

top.why: Insomnia affects most people with bothersome tinnitus; a 2023 RCT (N=102) showed clinically meaningful insomnia improvement in >80% with CBT-I vs 47% and 20% in two active control arms, with tinnitus distress improving too.

detail.strongest: Well-designed three-arm RCT against ACTIVE controls with effects sustained at 6 months.
detail.weakest: Single center, single trial; tinnitus outcomes were secondary.
detail.studies: One adequately powered RCT (UCL/Barts 2023) plus strong imported evidence from the general insomnia literature.
detail.replication: Not yet replicated in tinnitus populations.
detail.distress: Moderate — large insomnia effect; tinnitus distress (secondary) improved and held at 6 months.
detail.availability: Available through sleep clinics and digital CBT-I programs.
detail.uncertainty: Whether results generalize beyond the single UK center.

top.couldChange: Replication outside the single UK center would raise confidence.

top.why: Pooled THI reduction of −17.7 points vs untreated controls across 3 RCTs; a plausible, safe alternative to classic CBT with growing evidence.

detail.strongest: Meta-analysis of 3 RCTs: pooled THI −17.7 (95% CI −23.5 to −11.8); Westin 2011 d=1.04 vs waitlist.
detail.weakest: Only ~100 pooled participants; comparisons are mostly against no treatment.
detail.studies: 3 randomized trials pooled, from more than one group.
detail.replication: Some — Swedish and later international trials.
detail.distress: Moderate — large effects vs untreated controls.
detail.availability: Available where ACT-trained therapists exist; some digital versions.
detail.uncertainty: Performance against active controls and at scale.

top.couldChange: Larger independent trials; currently ~100 pooled participants.

top.why: Best-tested mindfulness approach: MBCT beat an intensity-matched active relaxation control by 6.3 TQ points post-treatment and 7.2 points at 6-month follow-up — a tougher comparison than most of this field attempts.

detail.strongest: Beat an ACTIVE control with a durable effect (6.3 points post, 7.2 at 6 months) — rare in this field.
detail.weakest: One main RCT (N=75); the reliable-change responder difference (59% vs 44%) was not statistically significant.
detail.studies: McKenna 2017 RCT plus smaller mindfulness trials.
detail.replication: Limited; an online iMBCT RCT is underway (Warsaw).
detail.loudness: None — loudness ratings improved equally in both arms (non-specific).
detail.availability: Generic MBCT is widespread; tinnitus-specific programs are rarer.
detail.uncertainty: Whether the effect survives online delivery and non-specialist settings.

top.couldChange: Multicenter replication; results are from specialist psychology settings.

top.why: The honest #10: by sheer volume of sham-controlled evidence (29 RCTs, N=1,228 in the 2020 meta-analysis), rTMS outranks any pipeline drug with zero controlled tinnitus data. Framed plainly: consistent short-term benefit over sham; durability disputed; effect sizes at or below clinical meaningfulness; not guideline-recommended.

detail.strongest: More sham-controlled RCT evidence than any other treatment on this list except CBT: THI −11.5 vs sham post-treatment (2025 meta, 16 RCTs, N=1,105).
detail.weakest: Durability: the 2020 meta found a small significant 6-month effect (−6.53), the stricter 2025 meta found none (−4.26, NS) — and both sit at/below the ~7-point meaningfulness threshold.
detail.studies: 29 RCTs (2020 meta) / 16 RCTs (2025 meta), independent academic groups worldwide.
detail.replication: Extensively replicated for the short-term effect; that is exactly why it earns the slot.
detail.distress: Limited — real but small and possibly transient.
detail.availability: Off-label at some centers; research settings; AAO-HNSF recommends against routine use.
detail.uncertainty: Whether navigated/personalized targeting (trials now recruiting) fixes the durability problem.

top.couldChange: A navigated-rTMS trial with durable 6-month benefit would move it up; another null durability meta would drop it out.

history.note: Initial Top-10 established at launch from the verified evidence base.

Phase 2 adversarial audit: Lenire and Shore/Auricle swapped (#2↔#3 — replication, authorization and availability outweigh one unreplicated trial; the old order was novelty bias). SPI-1005 removed from #10 (zero controlled tinnitus data — pipeline hype) and replaced by rTMS (29 sham-controlled RCTs, honestly framed). Every underlying claim re-verified against primary sources.
